question: What does incidence measure in a population?

options.A: The total number of existing cases
options.B: The proportion of people who have died
options.C: The total cost of treating a condition
options.D: The number of new disease cases

explanation: Incidence specifically counts newly developing cases of a condition over a given period, distinguishing it from total existing disease burden. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h1)

question: Why is tracking incidence useful for community health nurses?

options.A: It cures chronic illnesses in the community
options.B: It replaces the need for patient vital signs
options.C: It lowers the overall cost of hospital drugs
options.D: It helps detect disease outbreaks early

explanation: Monitoring new infections allows nurses and public health teams to spot rising transmission trends and respond before an epidemic grows. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h1)

question: Who should be excluded from the denominator when calculating incidence?

options.B: Healthy children under five years old
options.C: People who already have the disease

explanation: The denominator must only include individuals who are actually at risk of developing the condition, meaning they must be disease-free at the start. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h2)

question: What is the purpose of multiplying the final incidence fraction by a standard base like 1,000?

options.A: To account for inflation in medical treatment costs
options.B: To adjust the population size for missing census data
options.C: To inflate the actual number of sick patients for funding
options.D: To convert a tiny decimal into an easy-to-read whole number

explanation: Standard multipliers bring small rates into a readable format that can be easily compared across different populations. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h2)

question: What does prevalence measure that incidence does not?

options.C: All existing cases of a disease

explanation: Prevalence captures the total burden by counting both long-standing chronic cases and newly diagnosed ones together. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h3)

question: A researcher wants to know the total burden of chronic hypertension in a Nigerian state to plan medication supplies. Which measure is most appropriate?
explanation: Prevalence tells health planners how many total people need ongoing treatment, which directly guides drug supply and clinic staffing. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h3)

question: What is cumulative incidence also known as?
explanation: Cumulative incidence estimates the probability or risk that an individual will develop the disease over a defined time interval. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h4)

question: When must a researcher use incidence density instead of cumulative incidence?

options.A: When every single patient stays in the community for the entire five-year study
options.B: When study participants enter at different times and are followed for varying periods
options.C: When the total population size is fixed and known down to the exact person
options.D: When the disease is non-infectious and completely disappears within a week

explanation: Incidence density utilizes person-time denominators, making it ideal when people drop out or join a study at different intervals. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h4)

question: Why might a community clinic suddenly record a higher incidence of malaria without any actual change in mosquito transmission?

options.A: A drop in the total number of pregnant women visiting the antenatal clinic
options.B: A sudden increase in the population size due to migration from rural areas
options.C: Patients refusing to take prescribed antimalarial medications from nurses
options.D: Introduction of rapid diagnostic test kits that uncover previously missed cases

explanation: Better diagnostic tools catch mild infections that previously went unrecorded, creating an apparent rise in incidence without increased transmission. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h5)

question: Which factor does NOT directly influence the true biological incidence of an infectious disease?

options.D: Level of herd immunity in the population

explanation: Diagnostic tools change how many cases are detected and recorded, but they do not alter whether a pathogen actually infects a person's body. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h5)

question: A community health nurse notices a sharp rise in cholera incidence during the rainy season. What is the most appropriate immediate nursing action?

options.A: Stopping all routine immunization clinics to focus solely on wound care
options.B: Waiting until the end of the year to write a comprehensive report for the ministry
options.C: Discharging all admitted patients to make room for incoming emergency cases
options.D: Initiating community water sanitation education and distributing oral rehydration supplies

explanation: A rising incidence of a waterborne disease requires immediate preventive education and emergency treatment supplies to halt transmission. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of public health disease surveillance systems?

options.A: To replace physical clinical examinations with computer algorithms
options.B: To punish hospitals that report high numbers of infectious patients
options.C: To track disease occurrences and guide timely public health interventions
options.D: To calculate exact financial profits for private pharmaceutical companies

explanation: Surveillance collects ongoing health data so authorities can detect threats early and deploy effective nursing and medical interventions. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h6)
